Therefore, PtL processes require enormous energy input to deoxygenate and elevate the energetic properties of the CO feedstock into something more 2 resembling a fuel. Due to this high intrinsic energy intensity, the economic viability of PtL is inextricably linked to the availability of high volume of low-cost (and low-carbon) energy sources to rebuild the single-carbon CO feedstock into high-molecular-weight, energy-rich 2 molecules. Furthermore, CO capture—particularly direct air capture—adds additional cost and 2 complexity to an already intricate front-end-loaded process requiring electrolyzers, CO capture 2 units, syngas conditioning, and synthesis reactors, all of which must operate at high utilization to achieve competitive economics. Although PtL is an “emerging technology” from a commercial deployment standpoint, it is important to note that some PtL fuels are already ASTM certified. For example, the PtL fuels produced via alcohol intermediates or FT synthesis are already covered under existing ASTM D7566 annexes (i.e., Annexes 1, 3, 5, 8). Currently, the commercial development of PtL SAF is driven by a combination of technology licensors, energy companies, startups, and government-backed entities. Leading players include companies specializing in e-fuel systems, such as Norsk e-Fuel and HIF Global, alongside technology providers, such as Johnson Matthey, Topsoe, Sasol, and Shell, working on reverse water-gas shift and FT e-fuel platforms. The near-term outlook for PtL is driven heavily by the recent European ReFuelEU program, which mandates a growing share of synthetic aviation fuels, effectively guaranteeing demand for PtL SAF for as long as the mandates remain in place. Most forecasts anticipate the first wave of meaningful commercial PtL capacity coming online in the late 2020s, with significant scaling during the 2030s as renewable electricity prices fall and electrolyzer manufacturing expands. Despite high costs today, PtL is widely viewed as a critical long-term solution to improve the efficiency and energy security of the aviation sector by midcentury. 2.1.3 Jet A and SAF Distribution The method of moving fuels throughout the country depends on the location of production, fuel type, and volume. The modes of fuel transport include barge, tanker (ship), pipeline, rail, and truck (Figure 16). The U.S. fuel system is considered fungible, where multiple products share infrastructure. All modes have regulations and standards that ensure safe delivery of fuel meeting quality specifications. When SAF is blended into Jet A (as currently required) the resulting blend 21 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. is certified as meeting the ASTM D1655 standard for conventional jet fuel, and is therefore a fungible fuel. Jet fuel, including SAF blends, is tested for fuel quality at each movement across the supply chain. Jet fuel may pass through one or more terminals, and the quality is tested at the production location, each terminal, and the airport.
